I did not use to delegate anything on the technical side.

The company used to be six people in one room.
In 2019 we hired our first commercial director.
Before we talk about buyers, I want to talk about you. When you started, what did a Monday look like?
Long. We bootstrapped the whole thing, so there was never anybody else to do the work. I used to write the proposals, sign the contracts and run the interviews, all in the same week.
That was me as well. I used to be the only salesperson in my company for four years. Every Friday I would drive two hours to a client and come back the same night.
When did that stop for you?

When I made a hire I did not want to make. A commercial director, in 2018. I used to think nobody could sell what I had built, and I was wrong within two months. I was also about two months from burnout and I did not know the word yet.
I have the same blind spot. I still read every proposal.
Then here is the question a buyer will ask, and it is not about proposals. Who runs this company on the Monday after you step back?
Honestly, three people each own a piece of it. There is no single successor.

Say that out loud in the room. It is a better answer than an invented name. But say the rest of it too: what you used to do and what you no longer do. That is the only proof that the company has outgrown you, which is the compliment nobody enjoys hearing.
I used to approve every hire. I stopped last year. And I did not use to delegate anything on the technical side, and now I delegate all of it.
That is the sentence. Keep it in exactly that shape, and put a date on each half.
I used to write every proposal, and I stopped doing that in 2023.
We bootstrapped the company, so for years I would do all of it myself.
There is no single successor, and I would rather say that than invent a name.
I did not use to delegate anything on the technical side, and now I delegate all of it.
The company outgrew the way I used to run it, and that is the good news.

The mistake is almost universal, and it comes from pride, which makes it very hard to argue with. You ask a founder to describe his company and he describes everything he still does. He is in every important client meeting. He reviews the pricing on every large proposal. He knows the name of every person in the building. He thinks he is describing commitment. What the buyer hears is that this company has exactly one point of failure, and it is sitting across the table. So I give my clients twenty minutes and two lists. The first list is what you did every single week five years ago. The second is what you do every week now. The gap between those two lists is the entire story, and it is the only part of the story a buyer is actually paying for. And I have never once had a founder who could not fill the first list. The problem is never that nothing changed. The problem is that nobody ever asked them to say it out loud, so they have no sentence ready on the day it matters.

I have bought eleven founder-led businesses and I ask the same question in every one of them. I ask the founder what he stopped doing. Then, and this is the part that matters, I ask four other people in the company the same question about him, separately, and I compare the answers. A founder who still does everything himself is a price problem, and I can solve a price problem. What actually worries me is the founder who tells me he handed something over, and then three of his own people tell me they still bring that decision back to him. That is not a price problem. That is a man who believes something about his own company that is not true, and I will find twenty more of those beliefs after I have paid for it. And here is the one that surprises people. When a founder tells me there is no single successor, that three people each hold a piece of it, I trust him more, not less. Inventing a name is easy. The invented name never survives the second meeting.

Let me answer that with what changed, not with a name. We bootstrapped the company, so for years I used to do all of it myself. I used to approve every hire, and the team leads have decided that since 2025. I did not use to delegate anything technical, and now I delegate all of it. So there is no single successor. Three people each own a piece of it. And the one thing I still do that I should not is read every proposal.
